title: Condemned by Pilate, Crucified, and Buried
summary: At dawn the council hands Jesus to Pilate, and Judas, seized with remorse, throws the silver into the temple and hangs himself; the priests buy the potter's field with it. Pilate, warned by his wife's dream and pressed by the chief priests and the crowd, washes his hands, releases Barabbas, and hands Jesus over to be flogged and crucified. Mocked by soldiers, passersby, leaders, and fellow victims, Jesus dies with the cry of Psalm 22 on his lips; the temple curtain tears, the earth shakes, tombs open, and a centurion confesses him as the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea buries him, and the leaders have the tomb sealed and guarded.
story:
Chapter 26 ended with Jesus condemned by the council and Peter weeping. Now the story moves from the Jewish court to the Roman one, since only the governor could order an execution. The chapter is the center toward which all of Matthew has been heading since the angel told Joseph that Jesus would save his people from their sins (1:21). Its opening story of Judas stands beside the end of Peter's in chapter 26: two disciples who failed, one who wept and would be restored, one who despaired.

The chapter gathers threads from the start of the Gospel. The title King of the Jews, posted over the cross, is the title the Magi used when they came asking for the one born king of the Jews (2:2), and a Gentile centurion's confession answers those first Gentile worshipers. The taunt If You are the Son of God (verse 40) repeats the devil's words in the wilderness (4:3, 4:6), and Jesus again refuses to use his sonship to save himself. A dream warns a Gentile, as dreams warned Joseph and the Magi at the beginning (1:20, 2:12). The sealed and guarded tomb at the end sets the stage for the resurrection in chapter 28 and prepares Matthew's answer to the story that the body was stolen.
historical:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome as prefect from about AD 26 to 36, the title confirmed by a limestone block found in 1961 in the theater at Caesarea Maritima that records his dedication of a building to the emperor Tiberius. Philo (Embassy to Gaius 299-305) and Josephus (Jewish War 2.169-177, Antiquities 18.55-62 and 85-89) describe him as harsh and provocative toward Jewish sensibilities, though he could also back down before a determined crowd. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around 116, records that Christus was executed in the reign of Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate (Annals 15.44), and together with Josephus's paragraph on Jesus (Antiquities 18.63-64) this makes the crucifixion under Pilate one of the best attested facts of ancient history. Matthew calls Pilate simply the governor (hēgemōn) seven times in this chapter. The judgment seat (bēma, verse 19) was the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate gave formal verdicts, and the Praetorium (verse 27) was the governor's headquarters in Jerusalem, most likely Herod's former palace on the city's western side, though an older tradition places it at the Antonia fortress beside the temple.

The Passover amnesty of verse 15 is known only from the Gospels, but indirect evidence makes it plausible: the Mishnah allows a Passover lamb to be slaughtered for someone the authorities have promised to release from prison (m. Pesachim 8:6), and a papyrus from Egypt dated about AD 85 records a Roman prefect telling a prisoner that he deserved flogging but was being given to the crowds (Papyrus Florence 61). Matthew calls Barabbas a notorious prisoner (episēmos), and Mark says he was held with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising (Mark 15:7). The two men crucified with Jesus are lēstai (verse 38), a word that can mean robbers but that Josephus often uses for armed rebels.

Matthew alone tells what became of Judas and the silver. The priests would not put blood money into the temple treasury (korbanas), a scruple grounded in the principle of Deuteronomy 23:18 that wages gained by sin may not be brought into the house of the LORD, and they bought a potter's field as a burial ground for foreigners, pilgrims who died in Jerusalem far from home. Acts gives a different account in which Judas himself acquires a field, falls headlong, and bursts open, and the field is called Akeldama, Aramaic for Field of Blood (Acts 1:18-19). Harmonizing the two began early: a fragment of Papias, preserved by Apollinaris of Laodicea in the fourth century, tells of Judas surviving to swell grotesquely before he died. Since at least the fourth century Christian tradition has placed Akeldama at the lower end of the Hinnom Valley south of Jerusalem, where the Greek Orthodox monastery of Saint Onuphrius stands among rock-cut tombs; burial caves there, reused in the Roman period, were published by Gideon Avni and Zvi Greenhut (The Akeldama Tombs, 1996).

Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves, violent criminals, and rebels, designed to be slow, public, and shameful. Cicero called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty (Against Verres 2.5.165); Varus crucified two thousand Jewish rebels after Herod's death in 4 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 17.295), and during the siege of AD 70 Titus's soldiers crucified up to five hundred captured Jews a day (Jewish War 5.449-451). In 1968 an ossuary found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in north Jerusalem held the heel bone of a man named Yehohanan with an iron nail still through it, showing both that victims were nailed and that a crucified man could be buried in a family tomb.

The darkness of verse 45 drew comment from ancient writers. Julius Africanus, in the early third century, reports that the historian Thallus explained it as an eclipse of the sun, an explanation Africanus rejects because Passover fell at the full moon, when a solar eclipse is impossible (preserved in George Syncellus). Origen (Against Celsus 2.33) mentions an eclipse and earthquakes recorded under Tiberius by Phlegon of Tralles. Jewish and Christian sources also remember portents at the temple in the decades before its fall: Josephus tells of the massive eastern gate of the inner court opening by itself (Jewish War 6.293-296), the Talmud of the doors of the sanctuary opening by themselves during the last forty years (b. Yoma 39b), and Jerome reports that a gospel written in Hebrew letters spoke of the huge lintel of the temple breaking rather than the curtain tearing (Letter 120.8).
cultural:
Several details carry meaning a first reader would catch. Washing the hands to declare innocence of bloodshed echoes a Jewish rite: when a murdered body was found and the killer unknown, the elders of the nearest town washed their hands over a slain heifer and declared, “Our hands did not shed this blood” (Deuteronomy 21:7), and the psalmist washes his hands in innocence (Psalm 26:6, 73:13). In the Greek story of Susanna, Daniel cries out that he is innocent of her blood (Susanna 46), in words close to Pilate's. The crowd's reply uses a formula found throughout the Old Testament for accepting responsibility for a death: let his blood be on his own head (Joshua 2:19, 2 Samuel 1:16, compare Jeremiah 26:15), and the apostles are later accused of wanting to bring this man's blood on the high priests (Acts 5:28). The echo of the priests' words to Judas, You bear the responsibility (verse 4), in Pilate's words to the crowd (verse 24), shows each party trying to pass the blood to someone else.

Dreams were taken seriously as warnings in both Jewish and Roman culture; Roman writers told how Calpurnia dreamed of her husband's death the night before Julius Caesar was assassinated (Plutarch, Caesar 63; Suetonius, Julius 81). In Matthew dreams appear only at the beginning (1:20, 2:12, 2:13, 2:19, 2:22) and here, and each time they guide or warn in the matter of Jesus' life.

The soldiers' mockery parodies a royal investiture. Matthew's scarlet robe (chlamys kokkinē) was a soldier's short cloak, standing in for royal purple; the twisted thorns imitated a victor's wreath or a ruler's radiate crown; the staff was a mock scepter; and Hail, King of the Jews mimicked the salute to the emperor. Philo describes an Alexandrian crowd in AD 38 mocking the Jewish king Agrippa by dressing a harmless madman named Carabas with a papyrus crown and a mat for a robe and saluting him as lord (Against Flaccus 36-39). Simon of Cyrene (verse 32) came from a Greek city in North Africa with a large Jewish community, and Roman soldiers had the right to press civilians into service (compare 5:41). Golgotha is Aramaic for skull. The Babylonian Talmud records that a man led out to execution was given wine with frankincense to dull his senses (b. Sanhedrin 43a); Matthew calls the drink wine mixed with gall (cholē), wording that echoes the Greek of Psalm 69:21, where enemies give the sufferer gall for food, and Jesus tastes it and refuses. The clothes of the executed were the soldiers' perquisite, and the written charge (aitia) was posted to announce the crime.

The hours are counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon, the hour of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer in the temple (Acts 3:1). Matthew gives Jesus' cry in Hebrew, Eli, Eli, where Mark has the Aramaic Eloi; the Hebrew form makes the bystanders' confusion with Elijah (Eliyahu) easier to understand. Elijah, taken up without dying (2 Kings 2:11), was expected to return before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5) and was pictured as a helper of the righteous in distress. The temple had two great curtains, an outer one before the sanctuary and an inner one before the Most Holy Place, which the high priest entered once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16); Josephus describes the outer curtain as a Babylonian woven hanging that pictured the heavens (Jewish War 5.212-214, 219). A centurion commanded about eighty men. Burial before sunset was required by the law for anyone hanged (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), especially before a Sabbath, and a rock-cut tomb with a rolling stone was the kind of family tomb only the wealthy could afford. Sealing (verse 66) likely meant fixing cord or clay across the stone and stamping it, so that any tampering would show, as Daniel's den was sealed with the king's signet (Daniel 6:17).
literary:
Matthew follows Mark's outline but adds more of his own material here than anywhere else in the passion: the death of Judas and the potter's field (verses 3-10), the dream of Pilate's wife (19), the hand-washing and the crowd's cry (24-25), the earthquake, split rocks, and raised saints (51-53), and the guard at the tomb (62-66). Each addition serves one of his themes: fulfilled Scripture, the innocence of Jesus, the responsibility of those who condemned him, and the vindication that is coming.

The chapter is built as a series of trials and verdicts in which nearly everyone testifies, without meaning to, to who Jesus is. Judas calls his act betraying innocent blood; Pilate's wife calls Jesus that innocent man (literally that righteous one); Pilate asks what evil he has done and declares himself innocent of his blood; and at the cross the centurion and his soldiers confess him as the Son of God. The mockers speak truth without knowing it: he saved others and cannot save himself, because he will not. Their words, He trusts in God; let God deliver Him now, quote Psalm 22:8 and echo Wisdom of Solomon 2:18, where the wicked say that if the righteous man is God's son, God will help him. Their If You are the Son of God repeats the devil's test (4:3, 4:6). The crucifixion scene is saturated with Psalm 22, from the divided garments (22:18) and wagging heads (22:7) to the cry of forsakenness (22:1), and with Psalm 69 (the gall and the sour wine).

The fulfillment citation in verses 9 and 10, the last of Matthew's formula quotations, takes its words mainly from Zechariah 11:12-13, where a rejected shepherd is paid thirty pieces of silver and told to throw them to the potter in the house of the LORD, but its field and potter call to mind Jeremiah, who visited a potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1-12), broke a potter's jar in the Valley of Ben-hinnom where he foretold burials (19:1-13), and bought a field with silver as a sign of hope (32:6-15). Matthew credits the whole to Jeremiah. Mark 1:2-3 does something similar, joining Malachi and Isaiah under Isaiah's name, the more prominent prophet (see the text note below for the proposed solutions).

The signs at Jesus' death are arranged in a sequence of passive verbs, the curtain was torn, the earth was shaken, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, the bodies were raised, which Jewish usage would recognize as describing God's action. The language draws on Ezekiel 37:12-13 (“I will open your graves and bring you up from them”) and on Zechariah 14:4-5, where the Mount of Olives splits and the LORD comes with all his holy ones. The chapter ends quietly, with two women sitting opposite the tomb (verse 61) and the leaders sealing it, so that the watchers and the guards are both in place for the morning.

outline.t: Judas's remorse and death; the potter's field
The crucifixion and the mockery at the cross
Darkness, the death of Jesus, and the signs that follow

doctrines.note: The innocent one dies while the guilty Barabbas goes free, an exchange the church has long read as a picture of substitution. The blood the crowd calls down in verse 25 is the blood Jesus had called the blood of the covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28), and the torn curtain shows that his death opens the access to God that the Day of Atonement pointed to (Hebrews 10:19-20).

Jesus enters the depth of human suffering: injustice, humiliation, physical agony, abandonment by friends, and the experience of forsakenness voiced in Psalm 22:1. That he prays a psalm of lament from the cross gives his followers permission to bring their own darkest experiences to God in honest words.

Jesus is condemned and executed as King of the Jews and mocked as King of Israel (verses 11, 29, 37, 42). Matthew wants readers to see that the title is true: this is how Israel's Messiah reigns, from a cross, fulfilling the Scriptures of the rejected shepherd (Zechariah 11) and the righteous sufferer (Psalm 22).

At the moment of Jesus' death the curtain of the temple is torn from top to bottom (verse 51). The tearing signals both judgment on the temple, whose destruction Jesus foretold (24:2), and a new way into God's presence through Jesus' death, the theme Hebrews develops (Hebrews 9:11-12, 10:19-20).

The opened tombs and raised saints of verses 52-53 present Jesus' death and resurrection as the beginning of the resurrection of the dead that Ezekiel 37 and Daniel 12:2 promised. Whatever one concludes about the historical character of the report, its theological point is that the end-time raising of God's people begins with Christ, the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20-23).

words.note: Haima, blood. It occurs about ninety-seven times in the New Testament and eleven times in Matthew, five of them in this chapter (verses 4, 6, 8, 24, 25). The word binds the chapter together: innocent blood, blood money, the Field of Blood, Pilate's claim to be innocent of this man's blood, and the crowd's cry. In Matthew it recalls the righteous blood shed from Abel to Zechariah (23:35) and the blood of the covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28), which Hebrews says speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24).

Athōos, innocent, guiltless. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in this chapter: Judas confesses that he has betrayed innocent blood (verse 4), and Pilate declares himself innocent of this man's blood (verse 24). In the Greek Old Testament the phrase innocent blood translates the Hebrew dam naqi, used of blood whose shedding brings guilt on a land (Deuteronomy 19:10, 21:8-9; Jeremiah 26:15). Matthew's irony is that the guilty declare themselves innocent while only Judas names the truth about Jesus.

Metamellomai, to regret, change one's mind. It occurs six times in the New Testament, three in Matthew (21:29, 21:32, 27:3). It is not the usual word for repentance (metanoeō), and interpreters since the fathers have contrasted Judas's remorse, which drives him to despair, with Peter's bitter weeping, which leads to restoration; Paul distinguishes a worldly grief that produces death from a godly grief that leads to repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10). The verb need not mean that Judas's sorrow was insincere, but Matthew does not call it repentance.

Stauros, cross. It occurs twenty-seven times in the New Testament and five times in Matthew. Originally an upright stake, it became the instrument of Roman execution and, by the reversal of the gospel, the central sign of the Christian faith. Jesus had told his disciples to take up their cross and follow him (10:38, 16:24); here a stranger, Simon of Cyrene, is forced to carry his (verse 32), and the mockers twice demand that he come down from it (verses 40 and 42).

Egkataleipō, to forsake, abandon, leave behind. It occurs ten times in the New Testament and only here in Matthew, in Jesus' cry quoting Psalm 22:1, where the Greek Old Testament uses the same verb. The psalm begins in abandonment and ends in praise and the turning of the nations to the LORD (Psalm 22:22-31). Jesus' cry expresses real anguish, and many readers also hear in it the whole psalm's movement toward vindication, which begins at once in the centurion's confession.

Katapetasma, curtain, veil. It occurs six times in the New Testament: once in each Synoptic account of Jesus' death and three times in Hebrews (6:19, 9:3, 10:20). In the Greek Old Testament it names both the curtain before the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31-33) and the screen at the entrance of the sanctuary. Matthew does not say which curtain tore. Its tearing from top to bottom, from God's side, is read both as the opening of the way into God's presence and as a sign of judgment on the temple.

Egersis, rising, resurrection. It occurs only here in the New Testament, in verse 53, after Jesus' resurrection (literally, after his raising). It is the noun of egeirō, to raise, the verb the angel will use at the tomb (28:6-7). The phrase has puzzled readers because it seems to place the saints' coming out of the tombs after Jesus' resurrection though their tombs opened at his death; Matthew may be making the point that Christ must be the first to rise.

Koustōdia, guard, a loanword from the Latin custodia. It occurs only three times in the New Testament, all in Matthew (27:65, 27:66, 28:11). Its Latin origin suggests Roman soldiers, and the priests' promise to satisfy the governor (28:14) fits that; but Pilate's reply in verse 65, echete koustōdian, can be read either as you have a guard (your own temple police) or as take a guard (an imperative), and interpreters are divided.

christ:
This is the center of what Christ has done. The King of the Jews wears a crown of thorns; the Son of God, taunted to come down from the cross, stays there, and so saves others by not saving himself. The taunt If You are the Son of God repeats the devil's words in the wilderness (4:3, 4:6), and as there, Jesus refuses to use his sonship for his own rescue. He dies as the innocent one in place of the guilty, as Barabbas, a man condemned for violence, walks free. He dies as the righteous sufferer of Psalm 22 who trusts God and is mocked for it, as the rejected shepherd of Zechariah 11 whose price was thirty pieces of silver, and as the servant of Isaiah 53 who was silent before his accusers (Isaiah 53:7, compare verses 12-14) and was with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9, compare verse 57).

His cry, My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me, is real anguish, voiced in Scripture's own words by one who entered the full darkness of human abandonment. The church has understood it in several ways: as Jesus bearing the judgment due to sin (2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13), as the Son voicing the forsakenness of the humanity he took on, and as the first line of a psalm that ends in praise. Christians across traditions confess that the eternal union of Father and Son was not broken; the Son still cries My God.

The signs at his death announce what his death accomplishes. The torn curtain says that the way into God's presence, guarded for centuries, is now opened by his blood (Hebrews 10:19-20), and it also says that the temple's time is ending. The earthquake and the opened tombs say that death itself has begun to give way, that Christ's death and resurrection are the firstfruits of the general resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20). And the centurion's confession shows the nations beginning to turn to God, as the psalm Jesus prayed foresaw (Psalm 22:27) and as Jesus promised when he said that many would come from east and west (8:11). The Gospel that began with Gentile Magi seeking the king of the Jews now shows Gentile soldiers confessing the crucified king as the Son of God. The church confesses in the creed that he suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried, anchoring its faith in this public and datable event.
interpretation:
The chapter's special stories each took on a life of their own. Pilate's wife is unnamed in Matthew; the Gospel of Nicodemus (the Acts of Pilate, fourth or fifth century) calls her Procla and expands her dream, and Origen, in his commentary on Matthew, suggested she became a believer. The Eastern Orthodox Church commemorates her as Saint Procla on 27 October and the Ethiopian church on 25 June. Pilate's hand-washing made him a proverb for evading responsibility, while Tertullian (Apology 21) thought Pilate a Christian in his conscience, and the Ethiopian tradition came to honor him. Judas's death became the Western church's picture of despair, and medieval theologians contrasted his remorse with Peter's repentance.

The crowd's cry in verse 25 has the darkest history of any verse in Matthew. Melito of Sardis, in his Easter homily On the Pascha (around 160 to 170), already accused Israel of murdering God. Origen, in his commentary on Matthew (Series 124), taught that the blood of Jesus came not only on those then alive but on every later generation of Jews, and that reading became the common Christian interpretation for more than a millennium. It was preached in Holy Week, staged in passion plays (the Oberammergau play spoke the line from 1750 until it was cut for the 2000 season), and used to justify contempt, expulsions, and mob violence against Jewish communities, especially around Easter. After the Holocaust the churches reckoned with that history. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (28 October 1965, section 4) stated that what happened in the passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today, and that Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed as if this followed from Scripture; the Vatican's We Remember: A Reflection on the Shoah (1998) and many Protestant bodies, among them the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America in its 1994 repudiation of Luther's anti-Jewish writings, spoke in the same direction. Pope Benedict XVI (Jesus of Nazareth: Holy Week, 2011) argued that the Christian must remember that Jesus' blood speaks a different language from Abel's: not vengeance but reconciliation, poured out for many. Timothy Cargal (New Testament Studies, 1991) read the verse as a deliberate double meaning in which the blood that condemns is also the blood that forgives. When Mel Gibson's film The Passion of the Christ (2004) kept the line in Aramaic, he removed it from the subtitles.

The raised saints of verses 51 to 53 were read early as Christ's victory over death. Ignatius of Antioch, around 110, says that the prophets who waited for Christ were raised by him when he came (To the Magnesians 9.2), and the Gospel of Nicodemus expands the scene into the descent of Christ to the dead, the harrowing of hell, which became the Eastern icon of the resurrection, the Anastasis, in which Christ pulls Adam and Eve from their tombs. In 2010 Michael Licona's The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach proposed that the passage is probably apocalyptic imagery rather than a report of events; Norman Geisler's open letters charged him with denying inerrancy, and in 2011 Licona left his post with the Southern Baptist North American Mission Board, a controversy that made verses 52 and 53 a test case for how evangelicals think about genre.

In art and music the chapter is inexhaustible. Matthias Grünewald's Isenheim Altarpiece (1512 to 1516) shows the crucified body twisted by suffering; Bach's St Matthew Passion (1727) sets the whole chapter, with Paul Gerhardt's hymn O Sacred Head, Now Wounded (1656) as its recurring chorale and the brief chorus Truly this was God's Son as one of its most famous moments. The Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary read the chapter on Palm or Passion Sunday in Year A.
text:
Several differences among English Bibles come from the manuscripts. In verse 9 almost all manuscripts name Jeremiah, though the words come chiefly from Zechariah. A few later Greek manuscripts and some Latin and Syriac copies omit the name, and one or two substitute Zechariah; Augustine already knew copies that named no prophet (Harmony of the Gospels 3.7). Editors agree that Jeremiah is original and the other readings are corrections. The proposed solutions are several. Most modern commentators hold that Matthew combined Zechariah 11:12-13 with Jeremiah's potter and field (Jeremiah 18, 19, and 32) and named the greater prophet, as Mark 1:2 names Isaiah for a combined quotation. Augustine suggested that Matthew's memory supplied the wrong name and that the Spirit let it stand to show that the prophets speak with one voice. Jerome reported seeing the words in a Hebrew apocryphon of Jeremiah shown him by a member of the Nazarene sect (Commentary on Matthew 27:9). Others have proposed that Jeremiah stood first in some ancient orders of the prophets and so could name the scroll, an argument that rests on the order in b. Bava Batra 14b.

In verses 16 and 17 some manuscripts, including Codex Koridethi (Θ) and family 1, and some Syriac copies, give the prisoner's name as Jesus Barabbas, so that Pilate asks, Jesus Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ? Origen knew manuscripts with this reading and disliked it, and scribes may have deleted the name out of reverence. The Nestle-Aland Greek text prints Jesus in brackets, and the NIV and NRSV include it; most other versions do not. In verse 24 many manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, have Pilate say he is innocent of ‘the blood of this just person’, while Vaticanus and Bezae lack ‘just’. In verse 34 later manuscripts read ‘vinegar’ (oxos) for ‘wine’, assimilating to Psalm 69:21, and in verse 35 the King James Version adds a fulfillment quotation of Psalm 22:18 drawn from John 19:24, absent from the earliest manuscripts. In verse 49 Sinaiticus and Vaticanus add a sentence in which a soldier pierces Jesus' side and water and blood come out, which editors judge a very early insertion from John 19:34, since in John the piercing comes after death.

Translation choices also show. In verse 54 the centurion's words lack the article in Greek (theou huios), so some versions render ‘a son of God’ (NRSV margin) while most have ‘the Son of God’; Greek often omits the article before a predicate noun, and Matthew's readers would hear the full confession of 14:33 and 16:16. In verse 50 ‘yielded up the ghost’ (KJV) and ‘yielded up His spirit’ (BSB) render a phrase meaning literally he let go the spirit. In verse 65 ‘Ye have a watch’ (KJV) and ‘Take a guard’ (NRSV, ESV margin) reflect the two possible readings of echete. The chapter's naming of Mary the mother of James and Joseph (verse 56) appears as Joses in some manuscripts, as in Mark.

teach.big: The innocent Son of God, rejected by his people's leaders, condemned by Rome, and abandoned by his friends, dies in the place of the guilty, and God answers his death with signs that the way to God is open and death itself has begun to give way.

outline.t: The council hands Jesus to the governor: the human courts close ranks against him.
Judas's remorse without hope ends in despair, while God turns even blood money into the fulfillment of Scripture.
Jesus' silence before his accusers shows the servant who does not defend himself.
Pilate, his wife, the priests, and the crowd all have a part, and washing one's hands does not wash away responsibility; the guilty go free while the innocent is condemned.
The soldiers' mockery crowns the true King with thorns.
Every group mocks him, and their taunts proclaim the truth: he saves others by refusing to save himself.
In the darkness Jesus prays Psalm 22, entering human forsakenness to its depth.
God answers the death of his Son with a torn curtain, an earthquake, opened tombs, and a Gentile confession, while faithful women watch.
A rich disciple buries Jesus with honor, and the women see where he is laid.
The leaders' precautions against a resurrection end up guarding the evidence for it.

teach.pitfalls:
The gravest pitfall is to teach this chapter in a way that blames the Jewish people for the death of Jesus. Every teacher of verse 25 should know its history and say plainly that it does not make any people accursed. Present Pilate, the soldiers, the priests, the crowd, Judas, and the fleeing disciples as a gallery of humanity in which every reader finds himself. The opposite pitfall softens Pilate into a well-meaning bystander; Matthew shows a governor who knew Jesus was innocent and had him flogged and crucified anyway.

A second pitfall is to dwell on the physical horror of crucifixion as if the amount of pain were the gospel. Matthew describes the crucifixion in a few spare words and spends his attention on who Jesus is and what his death means. A third treats the cry of forsakenness either as proof that God abandoned Jesus in an absolute sense, dividing the Trinity, or as a mere quotation with no anguish in it. Both lose the text.

A fourth pitfall skips verses 51 to 53 because they are strange, or else uses them to settle debates about the intermediate state. They are Matthew's announcement that Jesus' death begins the resurrection of the dead, and teachers can say honestly that Christians differ on how literally to take their details. Finally, avoid reading verses 3 to 10 as a verdict on everyone who dies by suicide; Matthew tells what Judas did, and he does not pronounce on the fate of others who despair.
teach.pastoral: This chapter touches wounds that are present in every room. Judas's death touches anyone who has lost someone to suicide or who struggles with thoughts of it. Teach it with care, without speculation about anyone's eternal state, and say plainly that there is help: a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, or a crisis line such as 988 in the United States. Despair told Judas there was no way back, and Peter's story in the same pages shows that despair lies. The stripping and mockery of Jesus will reach people who have been abused or humiliated; they may find it healing that the Son of God knew that shame, and teachers should not treat it lightly. Those who feel forsaken by God can hear that Jesus prayed that very prayer from the cross. And Jewish listeners, or those with Jewish family, may hear verse 25 with fear because of how it has been used; name that history and reject it clearly.

hard.q: What does “His blood be on us and on our children” mean, and how should it be read after centuries of its use against Jews?
hard.a:
The objection is not only that the verse has been misused but that it may have been written to blame. Jewish scholars and many Christian historians note that Matthew alone includes it, that he writes after the war of AD 66 to 70 in bitter conflict with synagogue leaders (4:23, 10:17, 23:34), and that he shifts responsibility from the Roman governor who ordered the execution to all the people. John Dominic Crossan (Who Killed Jesus?, 1995) argued that such passages reflect later church-synagogue conflict rather than history. The verse's effects are beyond dispute. From Melito of Sardis in the second century and Origen's teaching that the blood rested on every later generation of Jews (Commentary on Matthew, Series 124), through medieval Holy Week preaching and passion plays, to the Christian soil in which modern antisemitism grew, the line was used to brand the Jewish people as Christ-killers and to justify contempt, expulsion, and violence. Jeremy Cohen (Christ Killers, 2007) traced that history. Some Jewish readers ask whether Christians should read the verse aloud at all.

Christian responses do not deny the history; they reject the reading. First, the crowd in Pilate's courtyard was a particular group on one morning, stirred up by particular leaders (verse 20), and it cannot speak for all Jews then or since; Pope Benedict XVI (Jesus of Nazareth: Holy Week, 2011) argued that it could not mean the whole people. Second, many modern commentators read our children as the generation that saw Jerusalem fall in AD 70, the judgment Jesus foretold on that generation (23:35-36, 24:2), a prophetic verdict on a city in history rather than a curse on a people forever. Third, Timothy Cargal (1991) and Benedict XVI both stress the irony that Matthew's readers could not miss: the blood the crowd calls down is the blood Jesus had just called the blood of the covenant poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (26:28), blood that speaks a better word than Abel's (Hebrews 12:24). Fourth, Matthew's Gospel is written by a Jew, about a Jewish Messiah, and its heroes and failures alike are Jews; the Roman governor, Roman soldiers, and all the disciples share responsibility in the same chapter. The church's own teaching has long said that the true cause of the passion is the sin of all humanity: the Roman Catechism (1566) taught that sinners of every age are its authors, Christians more than others. The Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965), the Vatican's We Remember (1998), and many Protestant statements have rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt. How much Matthew's own conflict with the synagogue shaped this scene remains debated among historians. That the verse gives no warrant for blaming the Jewish people, then or now, is the settled teaching of the churches.

hard.q: Did the earthquake and the raising of the saints (verses 51-53) really happen, or is Matthew using symbolic language?
hard.a:
The objection is historical. If many dead people rose and appeared in Jerusalem, it is striking that no other Gospel, no other New Testament writer, and no Jewish or Roman historian mentions it; Josephus, who records temple portents, is silent. The report also has an odd sequence, with tombs opened at Jesus' death but the saints coming out only after his resurrection, and its language closely matches Ezekiel 37:12-13 and Zechariah 14:4-5. Ancient historians used similar portents to mark the death of great men: Virgil's Georgics (book 1) lists a darkened sun, earthquakes, and ghosts seen at dusk at the death of Julius Caesar. On these grounds Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) treated the passage as a poetic, theological narrative drawn from popular tradition, and many critical scholars agree.

Christian interpreters answer in several ways. Many, including D. A. Carson and Norman Geisler, read the passage as a report of events, noting that Matthew narrates it in the same plain style as the surrounding history, that he says they appeared to many people as though witnesses could be asked, and that the silence of other sources is common in ancient history. John Wenham (Journal of Theological Studies, 1981) proposed punctuating verse 52 so that the earthquake and opened tombs belong to Good Friday and the raising and appearing to Easter, removing the odd interval. Others, including Michael Licona in The Resurrection of Jesus (2010), have suggested that Matthew uses apocalyptic imagery, a recognized ancient way of signaling that an event has cosmic significance, without intending every detail as a report; Licona argued that this is a question of genre, not of Scripture's truthfulness, though the dispute with Geisler that followed cost him his post. Still others hold that Matthew records a tradition he believed to be historical while shaping its telling from Ezekiel and Zechariah. The earliest Christian witness to the passage, Ignatius of Antioch around 110 (To the Magnesians 9.2), speaks of the prophets being raised by Christ, which shows it was read as an event.

This is a second-order question on which Christians who confess the bodily resurrection of Jesus hold different views. All agree on Matthew's point: Jesus' death and resurrection begin the resurrection of the dead that the prophets promised, and death's hold is broken.

observe: Who in this chapter declares or implies that Jesus is innocent, and in what words?
What do the passersby, the chief priests, and the robbers each say to Jesus on the cross?
What happens at the moment Jesus dies, and who responds to it, in what way?
interpret: Both Judas and Peter failed Jesus. What differences between their responses does Matthew show, and why do they end so differently?
Why do you think Matthew records the cry of forsakenness in its original language and connects it to Psalm 22?
What does the tearing of the temple curtain from top to bottom suggest about what Jesus' death accomplished?
apply: Pilate washed his hands and still handed Jesus over. Where are you tempted to think that declaring yourself uninvolved is the same as being innocent?
The mockers said he saved others but could not save himself. How does that truth change the way you think about power and love?
How might the psalms of lament help you bring your own darkest moments to God, as Jesus did?
